title: GPT-4 as a Homework Tutor can Improve Student Engagement and Learning Outcomes
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether GPT-4 can serve as an interactive homework tutor for secondary-school English language learning in a real school setting. The authors position the work as a response to the difficulty of scaling individualized feedback and corrective instruction for homework, especially in schools where teachers lack time to provide detailed follow-up. They specifically ask whether replacing traditional homework with GPT-4-based interactive tutoring can improve student learning outcomes and engagement.

The intervention used GPT-4 to deliver teacher-aligned interactive homework sessions. For each weekly exercise, the teacher supplied the pedagogical purpose, task description, and an example; these were used to prompt GPT-4 to run a tutoring-style dialogue rather than simply present static exercises. Students in the treatment group completed homework through GPT-4 chats on a dedicated website, while control students completed regular teacher-assigned homework on the same platform. The study used stratified random assignment within classes and collected both objective and subjective data, including pre/post multiple-choice tests and repeated questionnaires about engagement, usefulness, and student experience.

Participants were 75 students from four classes in one Italian technical high school, all taught by the same English teacher. Two classes were in the 3rd year (median age 16) and two in the 5th year (median age 18), all in a tourism track emphasizing business administration and foreign languages. The intervention targeted English as a second/foreign language homework outside class, while regular classroom teaching remained unchanged. The study was planned for 6 weeks and extended to 8 weeks due to curricular delays.

The authors conclude that GPT-4-based homework tutoring improved student engagement and produced modest learning benefits under some conditions. Overall learning gains favored treatment only weakly, but the 3rd-year cohort showed a larger, marginally significant benefit, while the 5th-year cohort showed essentially no difference. Treatment students rated homework as more interesting and better resourced, reported high satisfaction, and most wanted continued access to the tutor. The paper also reports very low observed hallucination/error rates in tutor interactions, but notes that benefits may depend on task type, with more objective grammar-style homework appearing better suited to this approach than open-ended essay tasks.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a real-world randomized controlled trial in a K-12 secondary-school setting with a clear comparator and quantitative outcomes, which is stronger than most current GenAI education studies. However, it has important concerns: under-review preprint status, modest sample size, incomplete reporting for some statistical details, cohort heterogeneity, and outcomes centered on English grammar/homework rather than the user's priority literacy constructs.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows at least medium-sized positive effects on engagement-related outcomes (d≈0.59) and a medium cohort-specific academic effect in 3rd year (d=0.603), even though overall academic effects were small/non-significant and 5th-year effects were null. Because some reported effects exceed 0.20 in a K-12 population, the paper meets the blue impact threshold overall, albeit with mixed academic impact.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4 delivered interactive English-as-a-second-language homework tutoring for Italian high-school students, replacing static teacher-assigned homework with chat-based guided practice, feedback, and step-by-step corrective support aligned to weekly classroom content.
Control students completed conventional online homework exercises on the same platform without GPT-4 tutoring; this functioned as a digital delivery channel for standard teacher-assigned homework.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports externally measured learning gains on English homework content via 24-item multiple-choice pre/post tests, with the strongest effects in 3rd-year classes focused largely on grammar-style objective exercises. Overall treatment-vs-control gains were small and non-significant (Cohen's d=0.251, p=0.314), but for 3rd year the effect favored GPT-4 and was marginally significant (d=0.603, p=0.087), while for 5th year there was essentially no difference (d=-0.004, p=0.991). This is an EFL language-learning study, not a direct reading-comprehension/vocabulary/reading-attitudes study.
finding.measure: 24-item teacher-authored multiple-choice pre-test/post-test on English content covered during the intervention; learning gains by cohort/year
finding.study_size: n=75 total students (control n=39, treatment n=36); 3rd year n=39, 5th year n=37 as reported in class totals
finding.effect_size: overall d=0.251; 3rd year d=0.603; 5th year d=-0.004

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 homework tutoring improved several short-term engagement-related ratings relative to control homework. Students in the treatment group rated homework more interesting (d=0.593, p=0.011) and better resourced (d=0.586, p=0.015), while usefulness (d=0.356, p=0.125) and comprehensiveness (d=0.281, p=0.234) trended positive but were not statistically significant; additionally, 32/35 students wanted to continue using the tutor after the study.
finding.measure: Weekly Likert-scale questionnaires on interestingness, usefulness, comprehensiveness, level of resources; final survey acceptance/satisfaction items
finding.study_size: n=75 total students; final item denominators varied (e.g., 32/35, 32/33, 30/35, 26/34 treatment respondents)
finding.effect_size: interestingness d=0.593; level_of_resources d=0.586; usefulness d=0.356; comprehensiveness d=0.281

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed to minimize teacher preparation burden by requiring only the normal homework components (purpose, description, example) to seed GPT-4, and the teacher reported that after an initial learning curve the system could somewhat reduce workload in the long term. However, no formal workload timing study or quantitative efficiency metric was reported, so evidence on efficiency is suggestive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Teacher post-study feedback about workload and feasibility; implementation characteristics
